To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mass of an unstable particle in lattice simulations is not the real part of its pole position, but is the energy at which its scattering phase passes through the value π/2, and that the spectral weight is volume dependent and can be used to distinguish between one- and two-particle contributions in the lattice data.
the mass, width, and spectral weights are not necessarily the same for unstable particles in lattice QCD.

the energy at which a scattering phase crosses π/2 and the real part of a pole position for an unstable particle in a theory with a nontrivial S-matrix are not necessarily the same as the eigenvalues measured in Euclidean correlation functions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the issues of the spectral parameters (the mass and width) and spectral weights of unstable particles in Lattice QED and QCD.
the extraction of physical information about unstable particles from Euclidean lattice correlation functions.
the issues of how one can extract the mass and width of a resonance in lattice simulations and how one can identify the nature of the states in the spectrum.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in general, the spectral parameters (energy eigenvalues, mass and width) obtained from lattice calculations are not the same as the actual physical quantities.
the lattice QCD calculations of the spectrum of the unstable particles, such as the rho-meson, are not yet reliable.

the spectral parameters (energy, mass and width) of resonances are not well-defined quantities in lattice simulations and should therefore not be used in the interpretation of lattice calculations of resonances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spectral parameters and spectral weights of unstable particles in general are volume dependent.

the spectral parameters of unstable particles are not directly related to the pole positions of S-matrix elements, and that the spectral weights of the energy eigenstates are only useful for narrow resonances, and that they are not applicable for broad resonances.
the spectral weights of the energy eigenstates can be used to determine the mass of the unstable particles, provided that the resonance is sufficiently narrow.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spectral parameters obtained from lattice calculations are not the same as those used in phenomenology.
, for a broad resonance, the spectral weight of the eigenstate with energy closest to the resonance energy is not the same as the spectral weight of that eigenstate in the continuum limit.
one should not expect the spectral parameters (i.e., the pole positions in the S -matrix) to be the same as those obtained from the eigenvalues of a finite-volume Hamiltonian.
